--- title: "Co-Movement & Co-Crashes" subtitle: "Sectors, the correlation block, and the headline statistic" --- A portfolio's real danger is not that one name falls — it's that **many fall together**. This page shows that co-movement directly: which names share a fate, how the banks form a block, and what the course's headline *co-crash* number actually counts. --- ## 1 · The Correlation Block Order the basket by sector and the correlation matrix lights up in blocks. The five banks form a bright square (they move almost as one, ~0.77); utilities and staples sit in a dimmer corner, much less tied to the banks (~0.29) — though, as the next sections show, a systemic crisis lifts even those cross-sector links. ::: {#cell-fig-corr-block .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} order = meta.sort_values("sector").index.tolist() C = R[order].corr() # 14×14 Pearson matrix for the display C_mat: Float[Array, "n_assets n_assets"] = C.values fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 6.2)) im = ax.imshow(C_mat, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1) ax.set_xticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_xticklabels(order, rotation=90, fontsize=8) ax.set_yticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_yticklabels(order, fontsize=8) # sector dividers secs = meta.loc[order, "sector"].values bounds = [i for i in range(1, len(order)) if secs[i] != secs[i - 1]] for b in bounds: ax.axhline(b - 0.5, color=INK, lw=1.0); ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=INK, lw=1.0) fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label="correlation") ax.set_title("Correlation lives in sector blocks", fontsize=12) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Return correlation matrix, ordered by sector. The bank block (top-left) is uniformly bright — average within-bank correlation ~0.77 — while bank-vs-utility correlation averages ~0.29: far lower, but no longer negligible (the 2008 and 2020 crises couple everything to a degree). Sector membership still predicts co-movement.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-corr-block-output-1.png){#fig-corr-block width=863 height=728} ::: ::: That ordering isn't magic — it's just the `sector` column of the basket metadata. Before the matrix can light up in blocks, the tickers have to be *grouped* by sector. Here is that grouping made explicit: load the metadata and collapse it into a plain `sector → tickers` dictionary. Every block in this chapter (and every block the labs reload) is one entry of this mapping. ::: {#sector-grouping .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # meta is already loaded in the setup cell, indexed by ticker. # Re-read it un-indexed so we can group the `ticker` column by `sector`. meta_flat = datasets.load_basket_meta() sector_to_tickers = { sec: grp["ticker"].tolist() for sec, grp in meta_flat.groupby("sector", sort=False) } for sec, tickers in sector_to_tickers.items(): print(f"{sec:10s} → {tickers}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Banks → ['JPM', 'BAC', 'C', 'WFC', 'GS'] Tech → ['AAPL', 'MSFT', 'GOOG'] Energy → ['XOM', 'CVX'] Utilities → ['DUK', 'SO'] Staples → ['PG', 'KO'] ``` ::: ::: The matrix above is just this dictionary laid end to end: banks, then tech, then energy, utilities, and staples. The bright squares are the *within*-sector entries of the mapping; the dimmer off-diagonal rectangles are the *between*-sector ones. We will lean on exactly this distinction below. ## Blocks: From a Panel to Multidimensional Variables So far every quantity — a correlation, a co-crash fraction — has been built from *two scalar columns*. But the correlation matrix already hinted at something larger: a whole **sector** behaves like one object. Slice those columns out together and you get a **block** — a multidimensional variable $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, where $n$ is the number of trading days and $d$ is the number of names in the sector. A block is not a column; it is a *bundle* of columns you treat as a single variable. ::: {#sector-blocks .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # A sector is a block: select all of its columns at once. X_banks: Float[Array, "n_days d_banks"] = R[sector_to_tickers["Banks"]] # (n_days, 5) X_tech: Float[Array, "n_days d_tech"] = R[sector_to_tickers["Tech"]] # (n_days, 3) X_energy: Float[Array, "n_days d_energy"] = R[sector_to_tickers["Energy"]] # (n_days, 2) for name, blk in [("X_banks", X_banks), ("X_tech", X_tech), ("X_energy", X_energy)]: print(f"{name:9s} shape = {blk.shape} columns = {list(blk.columns)}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` X_banks shape = (4778, 5) columns = ['JPM', 'BAC', 'C', 'WFC', 'GS'] X_tech shape = (4778, 3) columns = ['AAPL', 'MSFT', 'GOOG'] X_energy shape = (4778, 2) columns = ['XOM', 'CVX'] ``` ::: ::: Read the shapes carefully: `X_banks` is `(n_days, 5)` — five real numbers per day, a point in $\mathbb{R}^5$, not a scalar. That single change of viewpoint splits every dependence question cleanly in two: - **Within a block** — *how redundant are the banks?* JPM, BAC, C, WFC and GS carry overlapping information; a within-block measure (later: **total correlation** $T(X_\text{banks})$) quantifies that shared core. - **Between blocks** — *how much do banks and energy move together?* That is a between-block measure (later: **mutual information** $I(X_\text{banks}; X_\text{energy})$) — one number summarising a $5 \times 2$ slab of the correlation matrix, not a single cell. Correlation can only ever fill one cell at a time. The information-theoretic measures in the dependence and gaussianization chapters take a *whole block* as their argument — which is exactly why those labs need blocks handed to them, not columns. ### The Real-Toy Block: Two Banks vs Two Energy Majors The full bank block lives in $\mathbb{R}^5$ — too wide to follow by hand. So we keep a deliberately small **real-toy block**: two banks against two energy majors, a real `[x1, x2, y1, y2]` panel you can read row by row. It is real market data, but small enough to reason about like a toy. ::: {#cell-real-toy-block .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} x: Float[Array, "n_days d_x"] = R[["JPM", "BAC"]] # block x: two banks → (n_days, 2) y: Float[Array, "n_days d_y"] = R[["XOM", "CVX"]] # block y: two energy majors → (n_days, 2) toy: Float[Array, "n_days 4"] = pd.concat([x, y], axis=1) # the [JPM, BAC, XOM, CVX] panel print("x shape =", x.shape, " y shape =", y.shape, " toy shape =", toy.shape) toy.head().round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x shape = (4778, 2) y shape = (4778, 2) toy shape = (4778, 4) ``` ::: ::: {#real-toy-block .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Now the 4×4 correlation of that little panel. This is the structure the information labs will later re-derive — and the *ordering* is the whole point: ::: {#cell-fig-toy-corr-block .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Corr(X) = (1/n)·ZᵀZ with Z = (X − μ)/σ (standardize columns, then gram) M: Float[Array, "n_days 4"] = toy.to_numpy() n_days = M.shape[0] μ = M.mean(axis=0) # per-column mean μⱼ σ = M.std(axis=0) # per-column std σⱼ (population, ddof=0) Z: Float[Array, "n_days 4"] = (M - μ) / σ # standardized columns, ⟨zⱼ⟩=0, Var(zⱼ)=1 Ctoy: Float[Array, "4 4"] = einx.dot("n i, n j -> i j", Z, Z) / n_days # ρᵢⱼ = (1/n)·zᵢ·zⱼ fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.6)) im = ax.imshow(Ctoy, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1) ax.set_xticks(range(4)); ax.set_xticklabels(toy.columns, fontsize=10) ax.set_yticks(range(4)); ax.set_yticklabels(toy.columns, fontsize=10) ax.axhline(1.5, color=INK, lw=1.2); ax.axvline(1.5, color=INK, lw=1.2) # x | y divider for i in range(4): for j in range(4): ax.text(j, i, f"{Ctoy[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", color=INK if abs(Ctoy[i, j]) < 0.6 else "white", fontsize=9) fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label="correlation") ax.set_title("within-bank & within-energy high,\nbank↔energy lower", fontsize=11) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The 4×4 correlation block of the real-toy panel [JPM, BAC, XOM, CVX]. Two bright 2×2 squares on the diagonal — within-banks (JPM·BAC ≈ 0.83) and within-energy (XOM·CVX ≈ 0.78) — and a dimmer off-diagonal 2×2 slab coupling banks to energy (≈ 0.35). Read as information: redundancy *within* a sector outweighs the shared signal *between* sectors — the ordering the labs quantify as T(x) within banks > I(x;y) banks↔energy.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-toy-corr-block-output-1.png){#fig-toy-corr-block width=622 height=510} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Block vs Column, in One Sentence A **column** is a scalar variable (one name's return). A **block** is a multidimensional variable (a sector, or a hand-picked bundle). Pearson correlation compares columns; the information measures ahead compare *blocks* — so this chapter's job is to build and hand off the blocks. ::: ## 2 · Co-Movement Up Close: Two Scatters Correlation is an average over all days. Zoom into two pairs and the *shape* of the dependence appears. Two banks fall on a tight diagonal — and crucially their points pile into the **lower-left quadrant** (both down hard on the same day). A bank and a utility make a diffuse cloud whose danger corner is far sparser — though, in this crisis-spanning sample, not empty. ::: {#cell-fig-scatters .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} def lower_tail_box(ax, x: Float[Array, "n_days"], y: Float[Array, "n_days"], q=0.10): tx, ty = np.quantile(x, q), np.quantile(y, q) # the q-quantile crash lines (qˣ, qʸ) ax.axvspan(x.min(), tx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08) ax.axhspan(y.min(), ty, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08) ax.axvline(tx, color=CRASH, lw=0.8, ls="--") ax.axhline(ty, color=CRASH, lw=0.8, ls="--") fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6)) for ax, b, name in [(axL, "BAC", "two banks"), (axR, "DUK", "bank vs utility")]: x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy() y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[b].to_numpy() lower_tail_box(ax, x, y) ax.scatter(x, y, s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none") cc = cocrash_fraction(x, y) ax.set_xlabel("JPM return"); ax.set_ylabel(f"{b} return") ax.set_title(f"JPM vs {b} ({name})\nco-crash = {cc:.0%}", fontsize=11) despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Daily returns, JPM vs BAC (two banks) and JPM vs DUK (bank vs utility). The shaded lower-left box is the joint-crash quadrant (both below their 10% tail). It is crowded for the banks (~70% co-crash) and far sparser — but not empty — for the bank-utility pair (~30%). Tail dependence you can see.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-scatters-output-1.png){#fig-scatters width=1304 height=538} ::: ::: ## 3 · The Co-Crash Number The statistic the course quotes again and again is the **co-crash fraction**: > Of the days when one name is in its worst 10%, on what fraction is the *other* > name also in its worst 10%? That is `cocrash_fraction(x, y)` — a conditional probability, $P(Y \text{ crashes} \mid X \text{ crashes})$. An **independent** pair scores ~10% (the threshold itself); a co-crashing pair scores far higher. Before tallying every name, watch the number built on a single pair. Take JPM and BAC, and shade the **10% of days JPM falls hardest** — that band *is* the condition. The co-crash fraction is then just a count inside the band: of those worst-JPM days, how many sit below BAC's crash line too (red), versus how many BAC shrugged off (blue)? ::: {#cell-fig-cocrash-anatomy .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy() y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["BAC"].to_numpy() qˣ, qʸ = np.quantile(x, 0.10), np.quantile(y, 0.10) # the 10% crash lines band: Float[Array, "n_days"] = x <= qˣ # condition: JPM in its worst 10% co: Float[Array, "n_days"] = band & (y <= qʸ) # …and BAC craters too → a co-crash hold: Float[Array, "n_days"] = band & (y > qʸ) # …but BAC held up fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 5.0)) ax.axvspan(x.min(), qˣ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.axhline(qʸ, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":") ax.scatter(x[~band], y[~band], s=7, c="0.78", alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(x[hold], y[hold], s=26, c=COOL, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none", label=f"JPM crashes, BAC holds ({int(hold.sum())})") ax.scatter(x[co], y[co], s=30, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label=f"both crash — a co-crash ({int(co.sum())})") ax.text(qˣ, ax.get_ylim()[1], " condition: JPM in its worst 10%", color=CRASH, fontsize=9, va="top", ha="left") ax.text(ax.get_xlim()[1], qʸ, "BAC's crash line ", color=INK, fontsize=8.5, va="bottom", ha="right") ax.set_xlabel("JPM return"); ax.set_ylabel("BAC return") ax.set_title(f"Of JPM's {int(band.sum())} worst days, BAC also craters on " f"{int(co.sum())} → co-crash {int(co.sum()) / int(band.sum()):.0%}", fontsize=11.5) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Anatomy of one co-crash number (JPM·BAC). The shaded band is the *condition* — the 10% of days JPM falls hardest. Among those days, red points fall below BAC's crash line too (a co-crash) and blue ones do not; their ratio is the co-crash fraction, here ~70%. The bar chart below runs this same tally for every name.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-cocrash-anatomy-output-1.png){#fig-cocrash-anatomy width=896 height=585} ::: ::: Run that same tally for **every** name against JPM and the contagion structure appears: ::: {#cell-fig-cocrash-bars .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} cc = (pd.Series({t: cocrash_fraction(R["JPM"].to_numpy(), R[t].to_numpy()) for t in R.columns if t != "JPM"}) .sort_values()) colors = [CRASH if meta.loc[t, "sector"] == "Banks" else plotting.PALETTE["green"] if meta.loc[t, "sector"] in ("Utilities", "Staples") else COOL for t in cc.index] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2)) ax.barh(cc.index, cc.values * 100, color=colors) ax.axvline(10, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)") ax.set_xlabel("co-crash with JPM (%)") ax.set_title("Banks crash hardest with JPM; defensives aren't immune", fontsize=12) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right"); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Co-crash fraction of every name with JPM. The other banks land near 65–70% (when JPM has a worst-10% day, so do they). Even defensive utilities sit at ~30% — three times the 10% independence baseline (dashed) — because systemic crises drag everyone down. But the banks still tower over the rest.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-cocrash-bars-output-1.png){#fig-cocrash-bars width=1004 height=489} ::: ::: ## 4 · More Than Correlation Predicts The 10% line is the wrong yardstick once names are correlated at all — a correlated pair *should* co-crash more than 10%. The sharper question: more than a **Gaussian** with that *exact* correlation would? Fit a bivariate normal to each pair's correlation and ask it the same co-crash question. Every pair beats it — even the diversified bank-utility pair crashes together more often than its correlation can account for. That surplus is genuine **tail dependence**: the part a covariance matrix, and the Gaussian risk model built on it, structurally misses. See it on one pair before totalling. Standardise JPM and BAC, then draw a bivariate Gaussian with their *exact* correlation beside the real cloud: ::: {#cell-fig-real-vs-gaussian .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy() y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["BAC"].to_numpy() xz: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (x - x.mean()) / x.std() # standardized JPM, z = (x−μ)/σ yz: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (y - y.mean()) / y.std() # standardized BAC ρ = np.corrcoef(xz, yz)[0, 1] # the pair's exact correlation rng = np.random.default_rng(0) g: Float[Array, "n_days 2"] = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, ρ], [ρ, 1]], size=len(xz)) LIM = 5 def _corner(ax, u: Float[Array, "n_days"], v: Float[Array, "n_days"], title): qᵘ, qᵛ = np.quantile(u, 0.10), np.quantile(v, 0.10) # the 10% crash lines box: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (u <= qᵘ) & (v <= qᵛ) # joint lower-tail quadrant ax.axvspan(-LIM, qᵘ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05) ax.axhspan(-LIM, qᵛ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05) ax.scatter(u[~box], v[~box], s=6, c="0.78", alpha=0.22, edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(u[box], v[box], s=13, c=CRASH, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none") ax.set_title(f"{title}\nco-crash = {cocrash_fraction(u, v):.0%}", fontsize=11) ax.set_xlim(-LIM, LIM); ax.set_ylim(-LIM, LIM) ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax) fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 5.0)) _corner(axL, xz, yz, "Real returns (JPM·BAC, standardized)") _corner(axR, g[:, 0], g[:, 1], f"A Gaussian, same r = {ρ:.2f}") fig.suptitle("Same correlation, same tilt — but real losses sprawl into the corner", fontsize=12) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Same correlation, two worlds (JPM·BAC). Left: real standardized returns. Right: a bivariate Gaussian fit to that exact correlation, r ≈ 0.83. Same tilt, same ellipse — but the Gaussian barely passes ±4σ, while real crashes sprawl past −10σ and pack the lower-left corner, so the real co-crash (~70%) outruns the Gaussian's (~60%). Axes clipped at ±5σ; the gap is tail dependence.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-real-vs-gaussian-output-1.png){#fig-real-vs-gaussian width=1244 height=592} ::: ::: The Gaussian is the right shape and the right tilt — it just can't reach the joint extremes the real corner is full of. Across pairs, that surplus is everywhere: ::: {#cell-fig-excess-tail .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal, norm def gaussian_cocrash(ρ, q=0.10): """Co-crash a bivariate normal with this correlation would produce.""" z = norm.ppf(q) return float(multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, ρ], [ρ, 1]]).cdf([z, z]) / q) pairs = [("JPM", "BAC", "JPM·BAC\n(two banks)"), ("JPM", "KO", "JPM·KO\n(bank · staple)"), ("JPM", "DUK", "JPM·DUK\n(bank · utility)")] labels, data, gauss = [], [], [] for x, y, lab in pairs: xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[x].to_numpy() yv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[y].to_numpy() ρ = np.corrcoef(xv, yv)[0, 1] # the pair's exact correlation labels.append(lab) data.append(cocrash_fraction(xv, yv) * 100) gauss.append(gaussian_cocrash(ρ) * 100) xs = np.arange(len(pairs)); w = 0.38 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2)) ax.bar(xs - w / 2, gauss, w, color=COOL, label="a Gaussian with the same correlation") ax.bar(xs + w / 2, data, w, color=CRASH, label="what actually happens") ax.axhline(10, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)") for i, (g, d) in enumerate(zip(gauss, data)): ax.annotate("", xy=(i + w / 2, d), xytext=(i + w / 2, g), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.1)) ax.text(i + w / 2 + 0.04, (g + d) / 2, f"+{d - g:.0f}", fontsize=9, color=INK, va="center") ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=10) ax.set_ylabel("co-crash (%)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 80) ax.set_title("Even a Gaussian fit to the exact correlation under-counts joint crashes", fontsize=11.5) ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right"); despine(ax) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Co-crash for three pairs: what a Gaussian fit to the pair's own correlation predicts (blue) versus what actually happens (red), against the 10% independence baseline (dashed). Every real pair lands above its Gaussian — by 6–11 points — so the joint crashing is not just 'they're correlated'. The gap is tail dependence the correlation never sees, and it survives even for the loosely-tied bank-utility pair.](04-co-movement-and-co-crashes_files/figure-html/fig-excess-tail-output-1.png){#fig-excess-tail width=1005 height=491} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Reconciling the Headline "56%" The same `cocrash_fraction` you see here is what the [gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) and [uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) labs report — there on a *controlled* synthetic co-crashing pair, where it lands near **56%**. On real bank pairs it is even higher (~70%); on a bank-utility pair it falls to ~30% — lower, but in this crisis-spanning sample even utilities are dragged well above independence. One definition, three datasets: | Pair | Co-crash | | |---|---|---| | Synthetic co-crashing pair (the labs) | ~56% | the teaching example | | Real bank pair (JPM, BAC) | ~70% | contagion in the wild | | Real bank-utility pair (JPM, DUK) | ~30% | dragged down in crises | | Independent baseline | ~10% | the threshold itself | The number is only meaningful next to its definition and its data. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Why This Drives the Course Pearson correlation already sees the bank block. What it *misses* is that the co-movement **concentrates in the tail** — the days you most need diversification are the days it vanishes. Catching that is the job of the [dependence](../dependence/index.qmd) measures and the reason Gaussian risk models fail in the [uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) chapter. ::: --- ## What the Labs Reload From Here The information-theoretic "Venn" labs — mutual information and total correlation between multidimensional blocks — **reload** the blocks defined above rather than re-deriving them. Below is the single, copy-pasteable recipe they start from: load the returns, build the sector blocks from the metadata, and build the real-toy `[JPM, BAC] · [XOM, CVX]` block. ::: {#cell-reload-recipe .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} from lectures import datasets R = datasets.load_returns() # (n_days, 14) panel of daily returns meta = datasets.load_basket_meta() # ticker → label, sector # Sector blocks: each sector is one multidimensional variable. sector_cols = { sec: meta.loc[meta.sector == sec, "ticker"].tolist() for sec in meta.sector.unique() } X_banks: Float[Array, "n_days d_banks"] = R[sector_cols["Banks"]] # (n_days, 5) X_energy: Float[Array, "n_days d_energy"] = R[sector_cols["Energy"]] # (n_days, 2) X_tech: Float[Array, "n_days d_tech"] = R[sector_cols["Tech"]] # (n_days, 3) # The real-toy block: 2 banks vs 2 energy majors — small enough to read by hand. x: Float[Array, "n_days d_x"] = R[["JPM", "BAC"]] # (n_days, 2) y: Float[Array, "n_days d_y"] = R[["XOM", "CVX"]] # (n_days, 2) print("sector blocks:", {k: R[v].shape for k, v in sector_cols.items()}) print("real-toy block: x", x.shape, " y", y.shape) pd.concat([x, y], axis=1).head(3).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sector blocks: {'Banks': (4778, 5), 'Tech': (4778, 3), 'Energy': (4778, 2), 'Utilities': (4778, 2), 'Staples': (4778, 2)} real-toy block: x (4778, 2) y (4778, 2) ``` ::: ::: {#reload-recipe .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
